paragraphs.context: The Moffats were very fashionable, and simple Meg was rather daunted
paragraphs.mainIdea: Meg enjoys the rich life at the Moffats' house and begins to copy them. She then feels poor and unhappy about her home.
paragraphs.simple: The Moffats were very fashionable, and Meg, who liked simple things, was a little afraid at first because the house was so grand and the people so elegant. But they were kind people in spite of their light, silly way of life, and soon made their guest feel at ease. Perhaps Meg felt, without knowing why, that they were not very educated or clever, and that all their show could not quite hide what they were really made of. It was certainly pleasant to eat rich food, ride in a fine carriage, wear her best dress every day and do nothing but enjoy herself. It suited her well, and soon she began to copy the manners and talk of the people around her. She put on small airs, used French words, curled her hair, made her dresses smaller and talked about fashion as well as she could. The more she saw of Annie Moffat's pretty things, the more she was jealous of her and wished to be rich. Now home looked bare and sad when she thought of it, and work seemed harder than ever. She felt she was a very poor girl who was badly treated, in spite of her new gloves and silk stockings.

sentences.context: she stood, like the jackdaw in the fable, enjoying her borrowed plumes
sentences.simple: She stood there enjoying the fine things that belonged to someone else, like the bird in the old story.
sentences.grammar: 'Like the jackdaw in the fable' is a comparison with an old story. A jackdaw is a bird that put on other birds' feathers to look fine. 'Borrowed plumes' means fine things that are not truly yours.

get up in style.meaning: To dress a person in fine, fashionable clothes.
